note: AAP and EducationHQ confirm tabling on 6 March 2024, the 1960-1994 scope, 23 other schools, four of six staff, more than 100 students (many 1971-72), boys usually 9-12, more than 120 people came forward, nine recommendations, the cover-up finding and the teacher moved to administration with a three-year ban. No changes.

fixes.d: In late May 2003 a woman told a Department of Families office that she had been sexually abused for 13 years in foster care by a family member who was an approved foster carer and by visitors to the household, and that other children placed with the family were also abused. In July 2003 the Premier referred concerns about the foster care system to the Crime and Misconduct Commission, which audited abuse notifications against current carers and held public hearings from 13 October 2003. Its report, released in January 2004, found the department's response 'completely inadequate' at most of nine points where children could have been protected, and concluded that the child protection system had failed Queensland children. It made 110 recommendations, including creating a separate Department of Child Safety and a Child Guardian.

note: Report summary confirms the May 2003 disclosure (sexual abuse, 13 years), the audit, hearings from 13 October 2003, nine 'flashpoints', the systemic failure finding and 110 recommendations; the CCC history page confirms the Premier's July 2003 referral. Changed 'sexually and physically abused' to 'sexually abused' (physical abuse is mentioned only for other children) and dated the referral.

CLAN catalogue confirms the November 2004 report, June 2006 Phase 2 report and the homes named; the Victorian redress summary confirms the 2003-2013 program, 1,848 eligible claimants and $35,000-$60,000 payments; Tasmanian Times (an opinion piece) is the source for the July 2003 trigger, sexual abuse from the early 1950s to the 1970s and the waiver of legal action; Canberra Times (27 Sept 2023) confirms the Commission of Inquiry finding. No changes; the waiver detail rests on the Tasmanian Times only.

cite: P. Parkinson, K. Oates, A. Jayakody, 'Study of Reported Child Sexual Abuse in the Anglican Church', commissioned by the Professional Standards Commission of the General Synod of the Anglican Church of Australia, May 2009 (full report, BishopAccountability.org copy); APO summary
note: Full report confirms every figure (17 of 23 dioceses, 191 cases, 180 complainants, 135 accused, ~65% clergy or candidates, three-quarters male, 23-year median delay, 8% not investigated, 44 court cases, 53% convictions); the APO page only has a short summary, so url switched to the full report. Removed y0/y1 because 1990-2008 is when complaints were reported, not when abuse happened (abuse was on average 23 years earlier).

fixes.d: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and finished in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', was released under the Official Information Act in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight.

note: NZFVC (27 Aug 2015) and NZ Law Society confirm 2008 set-up, the chair, 1,103 participants, pre-1992 scope, June 2015 close, the report title, quotes and sexual abuse. Removed the unsourced sentence about feeding into the Royal Commission and set y1 to 1991 (care 'before 1992').

gov.uk release confirms May 2014 opening, the 2007 Mill Hill inquiry, the 2013 NSPCC finding, the December 2016 Supreme Court refusal, the 4 August 2023 report, the 'straightforward or transparent' finding, no deliberate obstruction, KHT compliance case and the 67 allegations; Civil Society News confirms 'substantially constrained', the tribunal judge's 'ongoing risks' remark and over 1,000 congregations. No changes. Note: gov.uk marks this release as withdrawn on 10 September 2026 (still online); the Civil Society article is a backup.

fixes.cover: IOPC found significant failures by South Yorkshire Police to protect children from organised grooming; 8 officers had a case to answer for misconduct and 6 for gross misconduct; 43 of 164 complaint allegations were upheld
fixes.d: The Independent Office for Police Conduct published its Operation Linden report on 22 June 2022, after 91 investigations (begun 2014–2018) into South Yorkshire Police's response to child sexual exploitation in Rotherham from 1997 to 2013. The investigations covered 265 allegations from 51 complainants, 44 of them survivors, and the conduct of 47 officers. Eight officers had a case to answer for misconduct and six for gross misconduct; many had retired, five officers received sanctions from management action to a final written warning, and a sixth officer's misconduct case was found not proven at a 2022 hearing. The IOPC found the force was not equipped to deal with organised grooming at the scale it met in Rotherham and failed to protect vulnerable children.

note: IOPC release confirms all figures. Clarified that the 43 upheld were out of 164 complaint allegations, and reworded the sanctions sentence to match the release.

fixes.d: South Yorkshire's Police and Crime Commissioner, Alan Billings, commissioned Professor John Drew to review the force's handling of child sexual exploitation after concerns that Sheffield had seen failings similar to Rotherham's. The review, published on 23 March 2016, found the force had confronted 'a raft of weaknesses' in its earlier approach and had made strong progress over the previous three years. Drew said his picture was incomplete because he could not examine about 200 IPCC complaints about officers linked to Rotherham or speak to witnesses in ongoing criminal cases. The outgoing chief constable said the force had charged 124 people with child sexual exploitation offences since the 2014 Jay report.

note: Sheffield Telegraph (23 March 2016) confirms every fact; only change is attributing the 124-charged figure to the outgoing chief constable, as the article does.
